entry.title: Neuralink receives FDA approval for 'pivotal' brain implant trial in ALS patients (2 minute read)
entry.content:
Neuralink has received permission from the FDA to launch a trial for its LINK brain-computer interface. The study will be open to a limited number of patients with ALS in the US. It will evaluate patients' ability to control digital devices through thought and assess the system's long-term safety and reliability. If the technology proves to be safe, the trial may allow Neuralink to apply for more advanced trials and eventually release LINK onto the market.

entry.title: SpaceX Gets Approval to Launch One Million Satellites for Orbital Data Centers (4 minute read)
entry.content:
The FCC has granted SpaceX approval to launch a million data centers into space. Anthropic and Google have already committed to paying billions of dollars in fees to rent capacity from the network. Proponents of orbital data centers say offloading advanced computing to orbit will allow developers of AI tools to avoid the headaches they are facing on Earth. There are still numerous hurdles to overcome for SpaceX to deploy data centers in space. The FCC authorization gives SpaceX until 2033 to launch and operate the first satellite and until 2040 to launch the full constellation.

entry.title: The short age of dragon riders (10 minute read)
entry.content:
AI models available to the public have passed a threshold in August this year. They are now stronger than most theoretical physicists at most technical tasks. Models are now able to carry out complex analytical calculations, work out lengthy proofs, and turn well-posed problems into code with minimal input. There will still be joy in discoveries even if it is not only humans that push them.

entry.title: SpaceX is not a monopoly, tech incumbents obviously lack urgency, and other Harsh Truths (49 minute read)
entry.content:
The US space industry is generally unhealthy. The legacy industry lacks vigor. SpaceX's announced intention to gracefully sunset Falcon three years from now has induced a deep, spiraling panic among industry insiders who understand that there is no alternative. The company is uniquely positioned to put compute in space, and it has been investing heavily in this direction for more than a decade. Other tech giants have largely run out of ideas to invest for future growth. Due to this lack of vision, some have resorted to dividends and stock buybacks.

entry.title: Late Mid-Game Software Engineering (7 minute read)
entry.content:
There is a growing frontier of work that can be fully black-box automated. There is still some work that seems resistant to being automated, but once you have a reasonably verifiable target, then the work to get to that target largely falls to agent teams/swarms/factories. Agents' ability to do problem selection, intent, and taste is improving. This means a continuous rediscovery of what pieces require human input, and what can be fully given over, is required.

entry.title: Smart People Who Give a Shit Use Tools (11 minute read)
entry.content:
Lumping AI-using engineers in with the executives hollowing out their companies does real harm. Companies lose smart people who give a shit when they strip away ownership, punish dissent, and reward shipping volume over reliability. Give those same people real stakes, and a good model, and they won't check out. They will build the guardrails, proofs, and fixes they never had the hours to build before.

entry.content:
AI has been solving long-standing problems in mathematics at an increasing rate. These proofs come with formal certifications that prove their correctness to a level beyond what would normally be demanded for a math paper published in a journal. Many people will try to deny that these proofs are valid, but experts agree there aren't any real technical issues with the proofs. entry.title: The Most Famous Problem in Math Was Just Solved by AI—and This Human (10 minute read)
entry.content:
Levent Alpöge graduated from Harvard with the highest GPA in his class, won the prize for America's top young math researcher, and earned his Ph.D. in math from Princeton before he took a job at Anthropic. He recently stepped into the public limelight due to his claim of having solved the Riemann Hypothesis with the help of AI. His 17-million-line-long proof has already been verified by two independent groups. If it holds up to further scrutiny, Alpöge will become one of the most prominent mathematicians in history.

entry.title: Nightmare mode: simulating disk failures (20 minute read)

entry.title: The Incredible, Elegant DNA Repair System Makes Gene Editing Work (12 minute read)
entry.content:
Cells have a native repair mechanism for DNA that recognizes and replaces faulty DNA before lasting damage or dysfunction can set in. This ability evolved essentially at the same time as DNA, as it is impossible to have stable genetic information without DNA repair. The mechanisms are essential to the evolutionary lineage of all known life. Scientists and doctors experimenting with gene editing use these natural self-editing and repair tools to insert, delete, or mutate genes to study and treat disease.

entry.title: AI x Bio is not _just_ a data problem (14 minute read)
entry.content:
How far AI gets in biology will depend largely on how much data we have. It will also depend on what is measured and the quality of that data. An abundance of systematically incomplete measurements is unlikely to lead to a comprehensive understanding of many of the complex systems that occur in biology. AI will likely become a powerful tool that will contribute to the study of biology, but there is still no clear path to documenting a comprehensive account of how a whole cell or tissue works.

entry.title: The most important number in AI (42 minute read)
entry.content:
The Epoch Capabilities Index (ECI) is a measure of AI progress developed by Epoch AI, a nonprofit research organization. It provides a single number that summarizes how well AI models do on benchmarks. It is designed to be continuously updatable, and researchers can use it to look at trends going back years and forecast things for future models. This post covers how the ECI is constructed, the challenges of benchmark selection, whether it makes sense to talk about 'model IQ', whether static benchmarks stay relevant as models get better, and much more.

entry.title: Unblockable communication with gravity (32 minute read)
entry.content:
All modern wireless communication technologies are based on electromagnetism, which is readily susceptible to screening and blocking. Gravity is a viable platform for practically unblockable communication. This study proposes and implements a wireless communication protocol where a broadcaster encodes a binary message by moving a mass, and a receiver detects the resulting gravitational signal with an off-the-shelf, hand-held gravimeter.
